title: How To Teach Without Getting Stressed-Out; Arghhh!
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin shares his 'decide-first method' of stress relief, a technique he stumbled into as an overwhelmed student teacher and later found echoed in sports psychology advice about athletes managing competitive nerves. Rather than waiting until stress hits, the method requires deciding in advance, before students arrive, that nothing that happens that day will be allowed to affect the teacher emotionally. He describes a simple three-step morning ritual: sit quietly for a minute or two in the classroom, close the eyes and take deep breaths, then explicitly decide to remain calm and poised no matter what unfolds. Linsin argues that this decision-based composure spreads to students, producing calmer classrooms, more respectful student responses, and improved behavior, since students respond to and mirror a teacher's internal state.
points: The 'decide-first method' involves consciously deciding, before the school day begins, to stay emotionally unaffected no matter what happens.
Sports psychology supports the same principle: athletes who decide beforehand to keep composure despite adversity are more likely to do so.
The technique is a simple three-step ritual: sit in silence, take deep breaths, and explicitly decide to remain calm all day.
A teacher's calm internal state visibly spreads to students, who respond to and mirror what they sense from the teacher.
Practicing this method consistently is linked to improved student behavior and a teacher relying more on their classroom management plan than on force or persuasion.
quotes: I have a technique you can start using tomorrow that will eliminate stress from your teaching life. This no-stress method is so effective, in fact, that many professional athletes use it before a competition.

When I made the decision to become a teacher, I decided that I was going to love my job no matter the circumstances. I wasn’t going to sit back and see if I was going to be fulfilled, happy, or having fun.
The students began to feed off of my calm energy. And every day I gained greater control and respect.
He said that, before a match, if they will make a conscience decision to keep their composure—despite the adversity they may face—then remarkably, they will.
Being stress free in the classroom, as well as on the tennis court, is a decision you make. Stress doesn’t happen to you; you let it happen to you.
Your calm, confident demeanor will sweep the negative and excitable energy out of your classroom.
